sub_strands.sub_strand: Listening Comprehension (Theme 1: Child rights and responsibilities)
learning_experiences: listen to an oral narrative in pairs or groups,
identify words and phrases containing the sounds /ʌ/ /ɑː / from a print or audio text,
say words and phrases related to the theme accurately,
construct sentences using words and phrases with peers.
say tongue twisters containing the selected sounds collaboratively with peers,
write sentences and phrases containing the selected sounds and words,
make an audio recording of a poem containing the sounds /ʌ/ and /ɑː /,
play the audio recording and obtain feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we say the sounds in words, phrases, and sentences correctly?
How can we improve our pronunciation?
Why should we listen attentively?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration is developed as the learner works with peers to construct sentences.
Digital Literacy is enhanced when the learner uses electronic devices to listen and record themselves.
Learning to Learn is instilled as the learner adopts the use of correct pronunciation in various contexts for effective communication.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is inculcated as the learner learns about child rights and responsibilities, and practises them while making an audio recording of a poem containing the target sounds and playing the audio for effective feedback.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: Effective communication is achieved as the learner articulates the target sounds clearly and also listen to audio of the target sound.
sub_strands.links: The learner can link the content of child rights when they learn about child rights and responsibilities in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: recognise sounds /ʌ/ /ɑː /, words, and phrases correctly
use words and phrases related to the theme in sentences correctly
listen for the main idea and specific details for effective communication
respond to information from an oral text
adopt attentive listening for effective communication

skills.name: Use words about child rights and responsibilities
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word from the theme (right, responsibility, protect, education, shelter, health, safe, respect) to complete a sentence, and spots a sentence where one of them is misused, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up right and responsibility.

example.question: Every child has a ___ to go to school.

misconceptions.cause: Does not separate what you are given from what you must do.
misconceptions.reveals: right and responsibility in one sentence.
misconceptions.help: A right is something every child is entitled to. A responsibility is something you must do.
misconceptions.feedback: A right is something you are entitled to. A responsibility is a duty, something you must do.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a word with a related meaning that does not fit the sentence.

example.question: Parents should ___ their children from harm.

misconceptions.cause: Knows the topic words but not their exact meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Two theme words close in meaning.
misconceptions.help: Replace the gap with each word and test the meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: The word is related but does not fit the meaning. Try each word in the gap and check.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading (Theme 1: Child rights and responsibilities)
learning_experiences: select appropriate print and non-print reference materials (dictionaries, junior encyclopaedias, and, subject-specific encyclopaedias),
read selected reference materials independently,
look for information related to the theme from reference materials,
report and discuss what they have read with peers,
visit a library to find reference materials for information related to the theme.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do you read books?
Which type of books do you enjoy reading?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy is developed as the learner manipulates electronic reference materials for information.
Learning to Learn is nurtured when the learner uses reference materials to get information and furthers their learning process.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is developed as the learner does the assigned duty of selecting reading materials and reading independently.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: Interpersonal relationship is intensified when the learner learns about child rights and responsibilities and take upon their individual responsibilities both in school and at home.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses the skill on how to use reference materials in all the other learning areas as they all require searching for information.

outcomes.text: select relevant reference materials: dictionaries, junior encyclopaedias, and, subject-specific encyclopaedias on a variety of subjects
spell words correctly for effective communication
use reference materials to find the required information
adopt the use of reference materials for lifelong learning

skills.name: Choose and use reference materials
skills.mastery: Chooses the right reference book for a need (dictionary for meaning and spelling, atlas for places, encyclopaedia for facts), puts words in alphabetical order beyond the first letter, and uses guide words to decide whether a word is on a page, in 8 of 10 new questions.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses the wrong reference book for the need (an atlas for the meaning of a word).

example.question: Which book tells you the meaning of the word "harvest"?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know what each book is for.
misconceptions.reveals: A book that fits another need among the options.
misconceptions.help: Dictionary: meaning and spelling. Atlas: maps and places. Encyclopaedia: facts about a subject.
misconceptions.feedback: Each reference book has its own job. A dictionary gives meanings and spellings. An atlas gives maps. An encyclopaedia gives facts on a subject.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Sorts words by the first letter only.

example.question: Put in alphabetical order: bag, bat, back, ball.

misconceptions.cause: Stops when the first letters match.
misconceptions.reveals: Words that start with the same letter.
misconceptions.help: When the first letters match, look at the second letter, then the third.
misconceptions.feedback: When the first letters are the same, look at the second letter, then the third, to decide the order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Cannot use guide words to decide if a word is on the page.

example.question: Is "mango" on the page with guide words "maize" and "market"?

misconceptions.cause: Compares only the first letter, or does not know what guide words are.
misconceptions.reveals: A word that sits between the guide words alphabetically.
misconceptions.help: Guide words are the first and last words on the page. Everything on the page comes between them in alphabetical order.
misconceptions.feedback: Guide words show the first and last word on the page. Put your word in alphabetical order to see if it comes between them.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Class: Demonstrative Determiners (Theme 1: Child rights and responsibilities)
learning_experiences: identify demonstrative determiners: this, these, that, those, from a text s,
read sentences containing demonstrative determiners in print or electronic materials,
construct sentences using demonstrative determiners with peers,
make sentences containing demonstrative determiners from a substitution table,
use demonstrative determiners to fill gaps in sentences,
search for more examples of sentences containing demonstrative determiners in print and digital texts.
key_inquiry_questions: How do you identify objects that are near or far?
How do we show that objects being referred to are singular or more?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy is enhanced as the learner uses demonstrative determiners in sentences correctly.
Communication and Collaboration is achieved as the learner works with peers in constructing sentences using demonstrative determiners.
Digital Literacy is developed as the learner manipulates digital devices while searching for examples and usage of demonstrative determiners.
sub_strands.values: Respect is developed as the learner respects the opinion of others during activities involving peer engagement such as constructing sentences using demonstrative determiners.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: self-esteem in the learner is boosted as they learn how to communicate effectively using demonstrative with peers.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the knowledge gained in learning demonstrative determiners in learning Kiswahili and Indigenous Languages.

outcomes.text: identify demonstrative determiners: this, these, that, those, in a variety of texts
use demonstrative determiners: this, these, that, those correctly
promote the use of the correct demonstrative determiner to use during communication

skills.name: Use this, these, that and those
skills.mastery: Chooses or writes this, these, that or those so that it agrees in number with the noun and fits the distance (near or far), in 8 of 10 new sentences, and finds the one wrong demonstrative in a short note.

misconceptions.error: Uses this or that with a plural noun.

example.question: Look at ___ books on my desk.

misconceptions.cause: Learns "this" as the word for pointing and does not match it to singular or plural.
misconceptions.reveals: A plural noun after this/that, with the same sentence also offered with these/those.
misconceptions.help: Point to one object and say this, to two and say these. Say the noun first: one book, two books.
misconceptions.feedback: This and that go with ONE thing. For more than one thing, change the word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses these or those with a singular noun.
misconceptions.cause: Over-corrects after learning that "these" is the word for many things.
misconceptions.reveals: A singular noun with these/those among the options.
misconceptions.help: Count the things. One thing needs this or that.
misconceptions.feedback: These and those go with MORE THAN ONE thing. Here there is only one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up near words (this, these) and far words (that, those).

example.question: Mama is holding a cup. "___ cup is mine," she said.

misconceptions.cause: Does not use the position of the speaker to choose.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence that says where the thing is (in my hand, across the field).
misconceptions.help: Use this and these for things near you, that and those for things far away.
misconceptions.feedback: Think about where the thing is. This and these are near the speaker. That and those are far from the speaker.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes "them" in place of these or those in front of a noun.
misconceptions.cause: Them is heard in speech before a noun; it is a pronoun, not a pointing word.
misconceptions.reveals: The option "them" before a noun.
misconceptions.help: Them stands alone (Pass them to me). Before a noun use these or those.
misconceptions.feedback: Them cannot come before a noun. Use a pointing word: this, these, that or those.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; widespread in speech

sub_strands.sub_strand: Functional Writing: Filling Forms (Theme 1: Child rights and responsibilities)
learning_experiences: search for sample forms from the internet, individually,
select the information to be filled in a form collaboratively,
fill a form related to the theme using the following details: personal information, school information, parents’ /guardians’ details, religion/county information, favourite sport, hobby among others,
discuss the importance of filling forms correctly with peers,
design a form to obtain information with peers and upload it online.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we fill forms?
Why is it important to fill forms accurately?
What details do we fill in forms?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy is developed as the learner manipulates digital devices to upload forms on the internet.
Creativity and imagination is enhanced as the learner embraces ideas that inspire creativity when designing forms.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is fostered as the learner diligently designs a form based on the theme with peers.
sub_strands.pcis:
Life Skills Education- effective communication skills are developed as the learner discusses the importance of filling forms correctly with peers.
Social cohesion is enhanced as learners work jointly to accomplish tasks.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the content related to child rights and responsibilities which they learnt in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: record specific details: personal information, school information, parents’ /guardians’ details, religion/county information, favourite sport, hobby among others in a variety of forms
design a form to obtain the required information
acknowledge the importance of filling forms correctly

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 2: National celebrations)
learning_experiences: identify words with these sounds: /p/ /b/ from print materials such as newspapers, magazines,
listen to audio-visual recordings of dialogue containing the sounds /b/ /p/,
visualise saying tongue twisters with the sounds /b/ /p/,
discuss with peers the vocabulary used in the text and construct sentences using the vocabulary,
respond correctly to questions based on the dialogue.
Role plays the events depicted in the dialogue,
interpret gestures, eye contacts, and facial expressions correctly.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we listen carefully?
Why do we take turns when talking?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy is enhanced as the learner role plays and constructs sentences using learnt vocabulary.
Learning to Learn is advanced as the learner builds on their own learning by taking short notes from the text they have listened to.
Digital Literacy is developed as the learner listen to audio-visual recordings of words containing sounds /b/ and /p/ in real use.
sub_strands.values: Unity is fostered as the learner collaborates with others to engage in role play and answers questions related to the theme.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: effective communication and self-awareness are enhanced as the learner differentiates the sounds /b/ and /p/ to communicate clearly.
sub_strands.links: The learner can relate the content in pronunciation and effective listening to similar concepts as sounds are learnt in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify words, phrases, and sentences containing the target sounds/p/ /b/ from texts
construct sentences orally using words related to the theme
listen for the main idea and specific details for effective communication
interpret a speaker’s feelings and emotions (non-verbal cues) correctly during an oral presentation
realise the importance of non-verbal cues and appropriate word choice in communication

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading (Theme 2: National celebrations)
learning_experiences: make predictions of what a story is about; what happens next in a story using the title/pictures in a story,
infer the meaning of words from the context,
use their imagination to visualise the events in a story,
draw pictures, diagrams, or posters of events in the story,
read poems of not more than five stanzas.,
read a narrative of up to 400 words silently,
retell a narrative or recite a poem and create a video or audio recording of the story.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is the title of a poem or a story important?
How do we predict events in a story or poem?
How do we tell the meaning of unknown words in a story?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and imagination is advanced as the learner participates in activities such as predicting the story by use of pictures and visualising the event in the story as well as drawing pictures and posters on the events in the story.
Learning to Learn is achieved as the learner retells a narrative or recite a poem and create a video of the recording of the story.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism is promoted as the learner shows love for their country when they sing songs or recite poems related to national celebrations.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: effective communication is enhanced as the learner learns to communicate clearly through pictures or story-telling.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies reading skills in all other areas of learning as they all require reading for comprehension.

outcomes.text: identify characters, places, and events in a story for comprehension
predict events in a text for comprehension
respond correctly to factual and inferential questions for comprehension
use contextual clues to infer the meaning of words for comprehension
recommend appropriate reading techniques to peers

skills.name: Identify characters, places and events
skills.mastery: Names the characters and the places in a short story and puts its main events in the order they happened, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Predict what happens next
skills.mastery: Uses clues in the title and the story to choose the most likely next event, and says which clue supports it, in 8 of 10 new passages.
question_forms: choose the clue that supports it

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Answer factual questions from a text
skills.mastery: Finds an answer that is stated in the text, tells true from false and not stated, and does not pick a detail that sits near the answer, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Answer inferential questions from a text
skills.mastery: Works out what the text does not say outright (why a character acts, how they feel, what a clue means) and does not give an answer the text contradicts or merely repeats, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use context clues to find the meaning of a word
skills.mastery: Uses the words around an unfamiliar word to choose its meaning, and says which words gave the clue, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Names a place when asked for a character, or the other way round.

example.question: Who is the story mainly about?

misconceptions.cause: Picks a noun from the first sentence without checking its job.
misconceptions.reveals: A place and a person offered together.
misconceptions.help: A character is a person or animal that acts. A place is where the story happens.
misconceptions.feedback: A character is a person or animal in the story. A place is where it happens. Check which one the question asks for.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names a minor character as the main one.
misconceptions.cause: Picks the first name mentioned.
misconceptions.reveals: A character who appears briefly.
misconceptions.help: The main character is the one the story follows most.
misconceptions.feedback: The main character is the person the story is mostly about, not just the first one named.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts events in reverse order or starts from the most exciting event.

example.question: Put the events in the order they happened.

misconceptions.cause: Remembers the ending best.
misconceptions.reveals: The ending event offered first.
misconceptions.help: Go through the story from the start and number each event as it happens.
misconceptions.feedback: Go back to the story. Events are told in the order they happened. Look for words like first, then, after that and finally.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps two neighbouring events.

example.question: Put the events in the order they happened.

misconceptions.cause: Does not check each linking word.
misconceptions.reveals: Two events that are close together.
misconceptions.help: Look for time words like then, soon after, later.
misconceptions.feedback: Two of the events are the wrong way round. Check the time words in the story: then, after, later.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something that has no support in the text.
misconceptions.cause: Guesses from personal experience rather than the text.
misconceptions.reveals: A dramatic event with no clue in the passage.
misconceptions.help: Find a clue in the passage first, then predict.
misconceptions.feedback: A good prediction is based on a clue in the text. Look for the clue that points to it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something the text makes unlikely.

example.question: What will probably happen next?
example.wrong_answer: a prediction that goes against the text
example.correct_answer: a prediction that fits the text

misconceptions.cause: Does not reread the facts.
misconceptions.reveals: An event the passage rules out.
misconceptions.help: Check that the prediction does not go against what you have read.
misconceptions.feedback: This prediction goes against something the text already told us. Reread the clues.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says something that has already happened.
misconceptions.cause: Repeats the last sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: An option that repeats the end of the passage.
misconceptions.help: A prediction is about what is NOT yet told.
misconceptions.feedback: That has already happened in the story. A prediction is about what has not happened yet.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a detail from the passage that is nearby but does not answer the question.

example.question: What did Achieng buy at the market?

misconceptions.cause: Matches a word in the question to the same word in the passage.
misconceptions.reveals: A detail from the same sentence as the answer.
misconceptions.help: Find the exact sentence that answers the question. Check the wh- word.
misconceptions.feedback: This is in the passage, but it does not answer this question. Reread the question and find the exact sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says "true" for something the text does not say.

example.question: The passage says the bus was late. True, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Fills the gap with what seems likely.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence that sounds likely but is never written.
misconceptions.help: True means the passage says it. If you cannot find it, it is not stated.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage never says this. "Not stated" means you cannot find it in the text, even if it sounds likely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says "not stated" when the passage says the opposite.

example.question: The passage says Wafula walked to school. True, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Does not look for a sentence that contradicts the statement.
misconceptions.reveals: A statement the passage contradicts.
misconceptions.help: If the passage says the opposite, the statement is false.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage says something different, so the statement is false.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Answers from what the child knows, not from the passage.

example.question: How many people were at the meeting?

misconceptions.cause: Uses own experience instead of the text.
misconceptions.reveals: An answer that is true in life but different from the passage.
misconceptions.help: The passage is the authority. Find the sentence in it.
misconceptions.feedback: Answer from the passage, not from what you know. The text says something different.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Repeats a sentence from the text when asked to work something out.

example.question: Why do you think Mercy was smiling?

misconceptions.cause: Treats an inference question as a find-it question.
misconceptions.reveals: An answer copied from the passage that does not say why.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what clues does the text give? What do they show?
misconceptions.feedback: This repeats the passage but does not explain why. An inference question asks you to work it out from the clues.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an answer that goes against the text.

example.question: How did Otieno feel?
example.correct_answer: the feeling shown by the clues

misconceptions.cause: Takes one word and ignores the rest.
misconceptions.reveals: The opposite feeling offered beside the right one.
misconceptions.help: Check all the clues: what he said, what he did, what happened.
misconceptions.feedback: The clues in the passage show something different. Look at what the character says and does.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an answer that goes far beyond the clues.

example.question: What can you tell about Mama from the passage?

misconceptions.cause: Builds a story that the text does not support.
misconceptions.reveals: A dramatic reason with no clue in the passage.
misconceptions.help: An inference must be backed by something written in the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage does not give enough clues for this. A good inference is backed by what is written.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the word's commonest meaning instead of the one the passage needs.

example.question: In the passage, what does "bank" mean?

misconceptions.cause: Does not read the words around it.
misconceptions.reveals: The commonest meaning offered beside the right one.
misconceptions.help: Reread the sentence with each meaning in place of the word.
misconceptions.feedback: This is a meaning of the word, but it does not fit here. Try it in place of the word and see.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a meaning from how the word looks or sounds.
misconceptions.cause: Matches the word to a known word with a similar shape.
misconceptions.reveals: A distractor that sounds like the word.
misconceptions.help: Ignore the shape and read the clue words around it.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not guess from how the word looks. Look at the words around it for clues.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the opposite meaning.
misconceptions.cause: Misreads a "but" or "although" clue.
misconceptions.reveals: The opposite meaning offered.
misconceptions.help: Look for words like but, although, however. They flip the meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: The sentence has a clue word such as but or although. Check which way it points.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says false or not stated for something the passage does state, perhaps in different words.

example.question: The passage says Wafula walked to school. True, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Looks for the exact words and misses a rewording.
misconceptions.reveals: A true statement that rewords the passage.
misconceptions.help: Look for the idea, not the exact words.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage does say this, in different words. Look for the same idea, not the same words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says true for a statement the passage contradicts.

example.question: The passage says the bus was early. True, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Reads quickly and matches only the topic.
misconceptions.reveals: A statement that changes one detail of the passage.
misconceptions.help: Check each detail of the statement against the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: Check the details. The passage says something different from this statement.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses words that do not help to find the meaning.

example.question: Which words help you understand the word "ravenous"?

misconceptions.cause: Picks words next to the target word, not words about its meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Words from the same sentence that do not explain the word.
misconceptions.help: Ask: which words tell me what the word means?
misconceptions.feedback: These words are near the word, but they do not explain what it means. Look for words that tell more about it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names a different place from the story.

example.question: Where does the story take place?
example.wrong_answer: a different place in the story
example.correct_answer: the place named for the scene

misconceptions.cause: Remembers a place but not the one the question asks about.
misconceptions.reveals: Another place named in the passage.
misconceptions.help: Find the sentence that says where the event happened.
misconceptions.feedback: That place is in the story, but the event did not happen there. Find the sentence that tells where it happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Class: Collective Nouns/ Reflexive Pronouns (Theme 2: National celebrations)
learning_experiences: identify reflexive pronouns and collective nouns from print and digital texts,
watch a video clip in which collective nouns and reflexive pronouns (myself, ourselves) have been used in sentences,
team up to pick out collective nouns and reflexive pronouns,
construct sentences using collective nouns and reflexive pronouns,
create and complete crossword puzzles using collective nouns and reflexive pronouns.
key_inquiry_questions: How do you emphasise that you did something on your own?
Which words do you use to refer to a group of things or animals?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Collaboration is enhanced as the learner works with peers to pick out collective nouns and reflexive pronouns from a text.
Digital Literacy is enhanced as the learner watches a video clip featuring nouns and pronouns.
sub_strands.values: Respect is fostered as the learner appreciates others’ opinions when answering questions and creating crossword puzzles collaboratively.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skill (self-awareness) is promoted as the learner learns to communicate effectively using collective nouns and reflexive pronouns in real life.
sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the knowledge gained in learning collective nouns and reflexive pronouns to the same concepts taught in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify collective nouns and reflexive pronouns in texts
use collective nouns and reflexive pronouns in sentences correctly
adopt the use of collective and reflexive pronouns during communication

skills.name: Use collective nouns for groups
skills.mastery: Names the usual collective noun for a group of animals or things (a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a swarm of bees, a bunch of bananas, a school of fish) and does not use one group word for every group, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Use reflexive pronouns
skills.mastery: Uses myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves when the doer and the receiver are the same, and does not write hisself, theirselves or an object pronoun in their place, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the group word of one animal for another animal.

example.question: A ___ of cattle was crossing the road.

misconceptions.cause: Learns a few group words and uses one of them for every group.
misconceptions.reveals: The group word of a different animal as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Match a group word to the animal: flock of birds or sheep, herd of cattle, swarm of bees.
misconceptions.feedback: That group word belongs to different animals. Each kind of animal has its own group word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an animal group word for things (a herd of keys), or a thing group word for animals.

example.question: Wambui carried a ___ of bananas home.

misconceptions.cause: Treats collective nouns as one list for everything.
misconceptions.reveals: An animal group word offered for fruit, keys or books.
misconceptions.help: Bunch is for things that grow or hang together: bananas, keys, flowers.
misconceptions.feedback: That group word is for animals, not for things like fruit. Think about what is in the group.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out "of" after the collective noun.

example.question: We saw a flock birds on the roof.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili puts the group word and noun together without a small linking word.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence with "of" missing among the options.
misconceptions.help: Say the whole pattern: a flock OF birds, a herd OF cows.
misconceptions.feedback: A collective noun needs the little word "of" before the things it names.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Puts -s on the thing instead of using the group word, or writes the group word as plural when one group is meant.

example.question: Three ___ of sheep were on the hill.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see that "three" asks for the plural group word.
misconceptions.reveals: A number before the group word.
misconceptions.help: Count the groups, not the animals: one flock, three flocks.
misconceptions.feedback: The number tells you how many groups there are. More than one group needs the plural form of the group word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes hisself or theirselves.

example.question: Juma made the kite all by ___.

misconceptions.cause: Builds the word from his and their, which are the possessive words, instead of him and them.
misconceptions.reveals: hisself and theirselves among the options.
misconceptions.help: Say: himself, themselves. The first part is him and them.
misconceptions.feedback: The word is built from him and them: himself, themselves. Hisself and theirselves are not English words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses me, you, us or them where the doer and the receiver are the same person.
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili uses one verb form (ni-ji-) for this, so English needs a separate learned word.
misconceptions.reveals: A first or second person sentence where the doer is also the receiver.
misconceptions.help: If I do it to me, say myself. The word ends in self.
misconceptions.feedback: You did the action to yourself, so the word must end in -self or -selves.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes ourself, yourselfs or themself, or mixes one self with many people.
misconceptions.cause: Does not change self to selves for more than one person.
misconceptions.reveals: ourself and yourselfs among the options.
misconceptions.help: One person: self. More than one person: selves.
misconceptions.feedback: When the doer is more than one person, the word ends in -selves, not -self.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a reflexive pronoun for a different person (myself for he).
misconceptions.cause: Remembers that the word ends in self but not which person it matches.
misconceptions.reveals: A reflexive pronoun for the wrong person among the options.
misconceptions.help: Ask who did it. Amina is she, so herself.
misconceptions.feedback: The word must match the doer. Ask who did the action, then choose the -self word for that person.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Choose polite words and expressions
skills.mastery: Chooses the polite expression for a table or classroom situation (please, thank you, excuse me, may I, pardon, sorry) and the polite reply to thanks or an apology, in 8 of 10 new situations.

misconceptions.error: Uses a command where a polite request is needed.

example.question: At the table you want the salt. You say, "___."
example.correct_answer: Please may I have the salt

misconceptions.cause: Uses the shortest form from home language or speech.
misconceptions.reveals: A command beside a polite request.
misconceptions.help: Start with please, may I, or could you.
misconceptions.feedback: That sounds like a command. A polite request starts with "may I" or "could you", and says please.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong reply to thanks or sorry.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes up the replies to thanks and to apologies.
misconceptions.reveals: sorry offered as a reply to thank you.
misconceptions.help: Thank you: you are welcome. Sorry: that is all right.
misconceptions.feedback: Reply to thanks with "You are welcome" and to a sorry with "That is all right".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says sorry when excuse me is needed, or the other way round.

example.question: You want to pass in front of an adult. You say, "___."

misconceptions.cause: Does not separate asking for room from saying you are sorry.
misconceptions.reveals: sorry offered where you ask for something.
misconceptions.help: Excuse me: to ask, to pass, to interrupt. Sorry: when you have done something wrong.
misconceptions.feedback: Say "Excuse me" when you ask for room or want to speak. Say "Sorry" when you have made a mistake.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use too ... to and too ... for
skills.mastery: Completes and builds sentences with too + adjective + to + verb and too + adjective + for + person (too hot to drink, too heavy for me), and does not add for to or a that-clause, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Use must and should with an adverb
skills.mastery: Writes must or should followed by the base verb and an adverb of manner (You must speak politely), without to, -s, -ing or an adjective where the adverb belongs, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out "to" before the verb after too + adjective.

example.question: The bag was too heavy carry.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili joins the verb with ku-, so a separate small word feels unnecessary.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence with "to" missing.
misconceptions.help: Say the pattern: too + adjective + TO + verb.
misconceptions.feedback: After too + an adjective, the verb needs the word "to": too heavy to carry.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes "for to" or "for" before a verb.

example.question: The soup was too hot for to drink.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes the pattern too ... for (person) with too ... to (verb).
misconceptions.reveals: for to among the options.
misconceptions.help: Use for before a person (for me) and to before a verb (to drink).
misconceptions.feedback: Use "for" before a person and "to" before a verb. "For to" is not used together.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a that-clause after too, as in "too tired that he slept".

example.question: Otieno was too tired that he slept.

misconceptions.cause: Confuses too with so ... that.
misconceptions.reveals: A that-clause after too.
misconceptions.help: So tired THAT he slept. Too tired TO stay awake.
misconceptions.feedback: Too ... that is not used. Use so ... that, or too ... to.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the person after to instead of for (too heavy to me).

example.question: The box is too heavy to me to lift.

misconceptions.cause: Uses to for every person in a sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: to + person among the options.
misconceptions.help: Before a person, say for: for me, for him.
misconceptions.feedback: Before a person (me, him, the children) use "for", not "to".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes "to" after must or should.

example.question: You should to wash your hands.

misconceptions.cause: Copies the pattern want to, need to, have to.
misconceptions.reveals: must/should + to among the options.
misconceptions.help: Must and should go straight to the verb, with no to.
misconceptions.feedback: After must and should, the verb comes straight away. Do not add "to".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts -s, -ed or -ing on the verb after must or should.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks every verb must change for tense or number.
misconceptions.reveals: must/should + verb form among the options.
misconceptions.help: After must and should the verb never changes: must walk, she should walk.
misconceptions.feedback: After must and should, use the plain verb. It does not take -s, -ed or -ing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective where an adverb is needed (speak polite).

example.question: You must speak polite to elders.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili uses one word for both (kwa adabu / mpole), so the -ly change is not obvious.
misconceptions.reveals: The adjective in place of the adverb.
misconceptions.help: Ask: how must you speak? Politely. The word describes the verb, so it ends in -ly.
misconceptions.feedback: The word tells HOW you speak, so it must be an adverb. Adverbs of manner often end in -ly.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses should for a strict rule, or must for a gentle suggestion.

example.question: Passengers ___ wear a seat belt. It is the law.

misconceptions.cause: Treats must and should as the same word.
misconceptions.reveals: A rule or law next to should, and advice next to must.
misconceptions.help: Must is for rules and strong duty. Should is for advice.
misconceptions.feedback: Must is stronger. Use it for a rule or a law. Should is for advice.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: strength of must and should

skills.name: Use words about road safety
skills.mastery: Chooses the right road safety word (pedestrian, zebra crossing, speed limit, helmet, seat belt, pavement, signal) to complete a sentence, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a road word with a related meaning that does not fit.

misconceptions.reveals: Two road words that are close in meaning.
misconceptions.help: Pedestrian walks. Passenger rides.
misconceptions.feedback: The word is about roads, but it does not fit this meaning. A pedestrian walks; a passenger travels in a vehicle.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a word that sounds like the right one.

example.question: Cross the road at the zebra ___.

misconceptions.cause: Uses a word met elsewhere.
misconceptions.reveals: A word from American English or one with a similar sound.
misconceptions.help: Say the whole phrase: zebra crossing.
misconceptions.feedback: In Kenya we say "zebra crossing". Learn the whole phrase.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use possessive pronouns and their determiners
skills.mastery: Tells a possessive determiner (my, your, her, our, their) from a possessive pronoun (mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs), writes each in the right place and never writes her's, our's or their's, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Uses my, your, her, our or their when nothing follows the word.
misconceptions.cause: Does not see that my needs a noun after it.
misconceptions.reveals: A gap at the end of the sentence.
misconceptions.help: My bag, but the bag is mine. If no noun follows, use mine, yours, hers, ours or theirs.
misconceptions.feedback: My, your, her, our and their need a noun after them. When nothing follows, use mine, yours, hers, ours or theirs.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses mine, yours, ours or theirs in front of a noun.
misconceptions.cause: Learns the stand-alone forms and uses them everywhere.
misconceptions.reveals: A noun straight after the gap.
misconceptions.help: If a noun comes next, use my, your, her, our or their.
misconceptions.feedback: Mine, yours, hers, ours and theirs stand alone. Before a noun, use my, your, her, our or their.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes her's, our's, their's or your's.
misconceptions.cause: Copies the apostrophe from Juma's and Amina's.
misconceptions.reveals: her's, our's, their's among the options.
misconceptions.help: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: hers, ours, theirs, yours.
misconceptions.feedback: Possessive pronouns do not have an apostrophe. Write hers, ours, theirs and yours.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a possessive word for the wrong person (his for Mama).
misconceptions.cause: Does not link the possessive word to the owner.
misconceptions.reveals: A possessive for the wrong person.
misconceptions.help: Ask: whose keys? Mama is a woman, so her.
misconceptions.feedback: The word must match the owner. Ask whose it is, then choose the word for that person.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading: Fiction and Non Fiction Materials (Theme 5: Traditional foods)
learning_experiences: work jointly to select texts from a collection,
preview a text to determine suitability.
scan a text to pick out vocabulary words,
skim through reading materials for the main idea,
select fiction and non-fiction reading materials of between 1000-1250 words (both print and non-print),
read selected materials independently,
set up an after-school reading club where they meet regularly,
share reflections on the books read collaboratively.
key_inquiry_questions: What materials do you enjoy reading?
Why is it necessary to read many books?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration is enhanced as the learner sets up an after-school reading club where they meet regularly with peers to read.
Digital Literacy is attained as the learner sources for a variety of reading materials online.
Learning to Learn is developed as the learner engages in independent reading which enhances sourcing for information and lifetime learning.
sub_strands.values: Unity is developed as the learner respects self and others’ opinions when selecting and reading fiction and nonfiction materials collaboratively.
sub_strands.pcis: Social justice is enhanced as the learner practises living together through establishment of an after-school reading club.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies extensive reading in other learning areas like Kiswahili which emphasises on the same concept.

outcomes.text: select relevant reading materials from a collection of books
scan a text to obtain specific information
skim through digital or print texts to establish appropriateness and relevance
read a variety of materials for fluency
judge the appropriateness of a reading text on the basis of language and interest

skills.name: Scan for details and skim for the gist
skills.mastery: Finds a name, time, place or number in a notice or timetable by scanning, and says what a text is mostly about by skimming, in 8 of 10 new texts.
question_forms: skim: choose what it is about

misconceptions.error: Reads the whole text word by word instead of looking for the key word.

example.question: At what time does the bus leave?

misconceptions.cause: Does not know that scanning means looking for one key word.
misconceptions.reveals: A time near the right time in the notice.
misconceptions.help: Look for the key word (bus), then read only that line.
misconceptions.feedback: You need to find the key word first (such as bus), then read that line carefully.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads the nearest line and takes the detail from the wrong item.

example.question: Which day is the sports day?

misconceptions.cause: Matches the number or day without matching the item.
misconceptions.reveals: The detail beside another event in the same notice.
misconceptions.help: Match the key word of the question to the right line first.
misconceptions.feedback: That detail belongs to a different line. Find the line about this event, then read across.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says a text is about one detail, not what it is mostly about.

example.question: What is the notice mainly about?

misconceptions.cause: Stops after the first line.
misconceptions.reveals: A single detail offered as the topic.
misconceptions.help: Skim the title, first sentence and last sentence to find the gist.
misconceptions.feedback: This is one detail. Skimming means reading the title and first lines to find what the whole text is about.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Class: Adjectives (Theme 5: Traditional foods)
content_topics: Comparatives and superlative forms of (regular/irregular) adjectives
learning_experiences: describe items using the comparative and superlative forms of adjectives e.g. that window is bigger than this one,
change positive forms of regular and irregular adjectives to their comparative and superlative forms,
pick out adjectives of size, shape and age from a narrative or poem in collaboration with peers,
construct sentences featuring adjectives of size, shape and age,
fill gaps using adjectives in the correct order,
create a crossword puzzle using adjectives.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we compare things, people or events?
Which words are used to describe things or people?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination is enhanced as the learner creates crossword puzzles and make sentences based on adjectives.
Digital Literacy is achieved as the learner searches for various adjectives on the internet.
sub_strands.values: Peace is enhanced as the learner cooperate with peers to change positive forms of regular and irregular adjectives to superlative forms.
sub_strands.pcis:
Environmental Education is enhanced as the learner is exposed to information on traditional foods.
Hygiene and Nutrition is enhanced as the learner interacts with texts with content on traditional nutritious food.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses this knowledge on comparison of adjectives to learn the similar concepts in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify comparative and superlative forms of adjectives in a text
order adjectives in terms of size, shape and age appropriately
use the comparative and superlative forms of adjectives accurately
advocate the importance of using adjectives correctly in communication

skills.name: Use comparative and superlative adjectives
skills.mastery: Forms and uses -er/-est, more/most and the irregular forms good-better-best and bad-worse-worst, with than for two things and the for three or more, and avoids double comparatives (more taller) and gooder, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Put adjectives in order
skills.mastery: Places two or three adjectives before the noun in the usual order (opinion, size, age, shape, colour, material) and does not put the adjective after the noun as in Kiswahili, in 8 of 10 new phrases.

misconceptions.error: Uses more and -er together, or most and -est together.

example.question: Kamau is more taller than Baraka.

misconceptions.cause: Adds both signals to be sure the comparison is clear.
misconceptions.reveals: more/most together with -er/-est among the options.
misconceptions.help: One signal only: taller OR more careful.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only one: -er or more. Never both.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts -er or -est on a long adjective (beautifuler).

example.question: This is the ___ story I have read.

misconceptions.cause: Applies the short-word rule to every adjective.
misconceptions.reveals: A long adjective with -er or -est among the options.
misconceptions.help: Short words take -er/-est. Long words take more/most.
misconceptions.feedback: Long adjectives such as beautiful and interesting use more and most, not -er and -est.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes gooder, more better, badder or worser.

example.question: This mango is ___ than that one.

misconceptions.cause: Applies the regular rule to good and bad.
misconceptions.reveals: gooder, more better, badder among the options.
misconceptions.help: Good, better, best. Bad, worse, worst. Learn these three words by heart.
misconceptions.feedback: Good and bad are special. The words are good-better-best and bad-worse-worst.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes "that" or "then" instead of "than", or leaves it out.
misconceptions.cause: Than and then sound alike in fast speech.
misconceptions.reveals: then or that in place of than.
misconceptions.help: Than compares two things. Then tells us what happened next.
misconceptions.feedback: To compare two things, use "than". "Then" is about time.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the -est form to compare only two things, or the -er form for three or more.

example.question: Of the two sisters, Achieng is the ___.

misconceptions.cause: Does not count how many things are compared.
misconceptions.reveals: A comparison of exactly two (or of many) things.
misconceptions.help: Two things: -er. Three or more: -est, with the.
misconceptions.feedback: Count the things. For two, use the -er form. For three or more, use the -est form.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: strictness for two things

misconceptions.error: Spells the -er and -est forms wrongly (biger, happyer).

example.question: Mwende is ___ than her sister today.

misconceptions.cause: Does not double the last letter or change y to i.
misconceptions.reveals: A misspelt -er or -est form among the options.
misconceptions.help: Big has one vowel and one consonant at the end: bigger. Happy ends in y: happier.
misconceptions.feedback: Check the spelling before -er: a short word may double its last letter (bigger), and y changes to i (happier).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the adjective after the noun (a table big).
misconceptions.cause: In Kiswahili the adjective follows the noun (meza kubwa).
misconceptions.reveals: The adjective after the noun among the options.
misconceptions.help: In English the describing word goes in front of the noun: big table, red cup.
misconceptions.feedback: In English the adjective comes BEFORE the noun, not after it.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Puts shape or colour before size.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the usual order of describing words.
misconceptions.reveals: Colour or shape before size.
misconceptions.help: Usual order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, material. Size comes before colour.
misconceptions.feedback: Size comes before shape and colour: a small red hat, not a red small hat.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: order taught with size, shape and age

misconceptions.error: Puts age before size, or shape before age.
misconceptions.cause: Orders the words by the order they come to mind.
misconceptions.reveals: Age before size.
misconceptions.help: Size first, then age, then shape: a big old round stool.
misconceptions.feedback: Size comes first, then age, then shape: a big old round stool.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: order taught with size, shape and age

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing: Narrative Compositions (Theme 5: Traditional foods)
learning_experiences: brainstorm ideas for a narrative composition collaboratively with peers,
read samples of narrative compositions with peers,
identify the parts of a narrative composition,
compose a narrative of 120 -160 words individually or collaboratively,
practise writing own narratives,
listen or view a recording of a narrative and rewrite it in own words,
proofread each other’s work and give feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do you enjoy reading stories?
How do you make your composition interesting?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination is enhanced as the learner creates and writes stories.
Learning to learn is developed as the learner listens or view a recording of a narrative and re-write it in own words,
sub_strands.values: Patriotism is developed as learners create narrative compositions featuring traditional foods for different communities showing respect for each other.
sub_strands.pcis: Life skills (Assertiveness) is enhanced as the learner masters the art of creative writing and can freely express themselves via writing.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the knowledge about traditional food crops to other subjects such as Agriculture and Science and Technology which have similar concepts.

outcomes.text: identify the parts of a narrative composition
write coherently on different topics
create a narrative composition for self-expression
promote creativity in writing among peers

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 6: Jobs and occupations)
learning_experiences: reproduce appropriate patterns of stress and intonation in speech,
sort the statements and questions on the basis of rising or falling intonation collaboratively with peers,
practise saying words, phrases and sentences with the sounds /f/ and /v/,
say tongue twisters with the sounds /f/ and /v/ collaboratively,
watch a video of a dialogue in which statements and questions are used,
recite a choral verse with peers,
use the right intonation on a role play on telephone conversation,
sing songs featuring stress and intonation.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we pronounce sounds and words correctly?
Why do we raise or lower our voices when speaking?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration is achieved as the learner reproduces appropriate patterns of stress and intonation in speech.
Self-Efficacy is nurtured as the learner practises saying words, phrases and sentences with the sounds /f/ and /v/.
sub_strands.values: Respect is developed as the learner displays understanding and appreciation of others’ efforts as they practise saying tongue twisters with the sounds /f/ and /v/.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: Effective communication is promoted as the learner makes telephone conversations using appropriate stress and intonation for effective communication.
sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the concept of stress and intonation to Kiswahili and other languages that expose learners to stress and intonation.

outcomes.text: sort statements and questions based on rising and falling intonation
pronounce words and phrases with the target sounds /f/ and /v/, correctly
construct sentences orally using words related to the theme
use stress and intonation appropriately in statements and questions
advocate the need for correct stress and intonation in varied contexts

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading Comprehension Dialogues (Theme 6: Jobs and occupations)
learning_experiences: make connections between the characters in the text and the people they know,
relate events in the dialogue to their experiences,
read and role-play a dialogue of about 400 words collaboratively with peers,
pick out main ideas from the dialogue,
answer direct and inferential questions based on the dialogue,
infer the meaning of words from the context (for example, from words occurring before or after).
key_inquiry_questions: How can we guess the meaning of words?
What makes you a good reader?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication and Collaboration is achieved as the learner engages in role playing dialogues collaboratively with peers.
sub_strands.values: Unity is developed as the learner collaborates with peers to role play dialogues related to the theme.
sub_strands.pcis: Learner Support Programmes - Career guidance is emphasised when the learners read and role play a dialogue on job occupations collaboratively with peers.
sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the skill of reading for comprehension to all other areas of learning as they all require reading.

outcomes.text: select unfamiliar words and phrases from a reading text
use contextual clues to infer the meaning of words from a text
respond to direct and inferential questions for comprehension
relate events in the story to their own experience

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Class: Determiners: Quantifiers: (Theme 6: Jobs and occupations)
learning_experiences: read a passage related to the theme and identify quantifying determiners from the passage collaboratively,
match quantifying determiners with corresponding countable and uncountable nouns,
list quantifying determiners that can be used with both countable and uncountable nouns,
read sentences containing quantifying determiners from the internet with peers,
construct sentences using quantifying determiners with nouns with peers,
complete sentences by filling in gaps using the correct quantifying determiners.
key_inquiry_questions: Which words do we use to show amount or quantity?
Why is it important to tell the quantity of something?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-Efficacy is nurtured as the learner uses quantifying determiners in sentences correctly and learns to apply them in life.
Communication and Collaboration is achieved as the learner reads the sentences with quantifying determiners from the internet with peers.
Digital Literacy is developed as the learner uses the internet to look for sentences with quantifying determiners.
sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner accommodates diverse opinions from peers as they complete tasks involving the use of quantifiers.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: Effective communication is promoted as the learner practises using quantifiers correctly to enable them communicate effectively.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses the knowledge of quantifying determiners to learn similar concepts in language areas such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify quantifying determiners: few/ a few, little/ a little, a lot of/ lots of, each, all, enough, most, least in a variety of texts
use quantifying determiners few/ a few, little/ a little, a lot of/ lots of, each, all, enough, most, least appropriately in a variety of contexts
judge the appropriateness of quantifying determiners in oral and written texts

skills.name: Use few, a few, little and a little
skills.mastery: Chooses few or a few for things that can be counted and little or a little for things that cannot, and knows that few and little say "hardly any" while a few and a little say "some", in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Use a lot of, each, all, enough, most and least
skills.mastery: Chooses and places a lot of, lots of, each, all, enough, most and least correctly, with the right verb after each, and writes most of the learners (not most of learners), in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses few or a few with something that cannot be counted (few water).

example.question: There is ___ water in the jug.

misconceptions.cause: Does not ask whether the noun can be counted.
misconceptions.reveals: A noun such as water, milk, sugar or time.
misconceptions.help: Can you count it one by one? Books yes (few), water no (little).
misconceptions.feedback: You cannot count water, sugar or milk one by one, so use little, not few.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses little or a little with something that can be counted (little books).
misconceptions.cause: Learns "little" as the word for a small amount of anything.
misconceptions.reveals: A noun such as books, chairs, eggs or children.
misconceptions.help: Chairs can be counted, so few or a few.
misconceptions.feedback: You can count chairs one by one, so use few or a few, not little.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not tell few/little ("hardly any") from a few/a little ("some").

example.question: We have ___ eggs, so I can bake a small cake.

misconceptions.cause: Treats the little word "a" as unimportant.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence where the next part shows there is some (or hardly any).
misconceptions.help: "A few" means enough to do something. "Few" means hardly any.
misconceptions.feedback: Few and little mean "hardly any". A few and a little mean "some, enough to use". Read the rest of the sentence.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: depth expected at Grade 5

misconceptions.error: Uses much with countable nouns or many with uncountable nouns.

example.question: There are too ___ cars on this road.

misconceptions.cause: Does not ask whether the noun can be counted.
misconceptions.reveals: much and many offered together.
misconceptions.help: Many goes with things you can count; much goes with things you cannot.
misconceptions.feedback: Many goes with things you can count (cars). Much goes with things you cannot count (traffic, water).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a plural verb after each.

example.question: Each of the girls ___ a bag.

misconceptions.cause: Hears "girls" and chooses the plural verb.
misconceptions.reveals: each + a plural noun and a plural verb among the options.
misconceptions.help: Each means one at a time, so the verb is singular: each girl has.
misconceptions.feedback: Each means "one by one", so the verb is singular: has, is, was.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a singular noun after all (all the learner).
misconceptions.cause: Does not match the noun to a word that means "every one of many".
misconceptions.reveals: all + a singular noun among the options.
misconceptions.help: All means many, so the noun is plural: all the learners.
misconceptions.feedback: All talks about many, so the noun after it is plural.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts enough after the noun (water enough).

example.question: We do not have ___ for everyone.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili puts the describing word after the noun (chakula cha kutosha).
misconceptions.reveals: enough after the noun among the options.
misconceptions.help: Enough goes in front of a noun: enough food, enough chairs.
misconceptions.feedback: Put "enough" before the noun: enough food, enough chairs.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes most of learners or all of children, leaving out the.
misconceptions.cause: Drops the small word the after of.
misconceptions.reveals: most of + a plural noun with no the.
misconceptions.help: After most of, all of and each of, add the or a pronoun: most of THE learners, all of THEM.
misconceptions.feedback: After "most of" and "all of", you need "the" (or them, us): most of the learners.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses least for two things, or less where least is needed, or a lots of.

example.question: Of all the shops, this one sells the ___ sugar.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see the difference between comparing two and comparing many.
misconceptions.reveals: less and least offered together, or "a lots of".
misconceptions.help: Less compares two. Least compares three or more. We write a lot of or lots of, never a lots of.
misconceptions.feedback: Less compares two things; least compares three or more. And write "lots of", never "a lots of".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing: Pictorial Composition (Theme 6: Jobs and occupations)

arrange different pictures logically to write a story coherently,

What messages do pictures communicate?
sub_strands.core_competences:

sub_strands.values: Responsibility is achieved as the learner takes up assigned roles of creating and proofreading pictorial compositions.

sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the skills to similar concepts in Art and Craft drawing, and Social Studies which features interpretation of maps and charts.

outcomes.text: choose possible topics for pictorial compositions
create a composition based on the visuals or pictures

take turns to read a dialogue collaboratively,

say the target sounds as modelled from a recording,

key_inquiry_questions: Why should we pronounce sounds and words correctly?
Why should you give others a chance to speak?
How do you tell if someone is happy or sad?
sub_strands.core_competences:

Digital Literacy is developed as the learner interacts with digital devices while watching a video.
sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner exercises patience as they practise listening interactively, turn taking and correct use of non-verbal cues.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skill Education: effective communication is enhanced as the learner watches a video of conversation and sees how people to interrupt politely in real life conversations.
sub_strands.links: The learner can apply correct pronunciation to learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify words, phrases or sentences with the target sound: /ə/ and the diphthongs: /ɪə/ and /eɪ/ from a dialogue
construct sentences orally using words related to the theme
pronounce sounds correctly for accuracy in speech
use words and non-verbal cues to express different moods

learning_experiences: skim through reading materials to obtain the main idea,
preview texts to determine suitability and relevance,
scan materials for specific details collaboratively,

read the selected materials individually,
share reflections on the books read collaboratively,
keep a record of materials read.
key_inquiry_questions: What kind of information do you find in books?
Why is it necessary to read many books?
What do you consider when choosing a material to read?

Collaboration is enhanced as the learner scans materials for specific details collaboratively,
Learning to Learn is developed as the learner selects appropriate reading materials from a library.
sub_strands.values: Unity is enhanced as the learner cooperates and assists one another to select appropriate reading materials.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective Communication is realised in the learner as they read the selected materials individually.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the skill of extensive reading to select and read non-fiction materials in all the learning areas.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Tense: Future Time using will/shall (Theme 7: Learning through technology)
learning_experiences: pick sentences which express future time from a text,
make sentences from a substitution table,
answer questions on future time using will/shall collaboratively,
construct sentences using will/shall collaboratively,
role play activities they plan or wish to do in future with peers,
watch videos offline or online and identify sentences featuring future time with peers,
use computers, tablets or mobile phones to listen to audio materials featuring future time,
make predictions (on events, weather, among others) using will and shall,
create display charts with sentences which feature will and shall.
key_inquiry_questions: Which words do we use to show future time?
How do you tell that something will happen in the future?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration is enhanced as the learner expresses future plans using will and shall in pairs.
Self-efficacy is developed as the learner acquires the skill of making sentences about activities they plan do in future.
sub_strands.values: Social justice is developed as the learner shows democracy when they engage in role play activities to plan or wish for what to do in future.
sub_strands.pcis: Effective Communication is realised as the learner practises basic sentence structures that express the future that they will use in their daily communication.
sub_strands.links: The learner uses the concept of future time in other language areas such as Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify words that indicate future time using will and shall in sentences
use will and shall to express future time correctly
collaborate with others to determine the correctness and appropriateness of the tense used in own or provided texts

skills.name: Use will and shall for the future
skills.mastery: Writes will or shall followed by the base verb to talk about the future, and does not write will goes, will went, will going or a present tense where a future is meant, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Puts the past tense after will or shall (will went).
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the verb must show tense after will.
misconceptions.reveals: will/shall + a past form among the options.
misconceptions.help: Will already says the future. The verb after it stays plain: will go.
misconceptions.feedback: After will and shall, use the plain verb: will go. Will already shows the future.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to the verb after will (will goes).

example.question: My mother will ___ us a story tonight.

misconceptions.cause: Matches the verb to he/she/it even after will.
misconceptions.reveals: will + a verb with -s among the options.
misconceptions.help: After will the verb never changes: will tell.
misconceptions.feedback: After will and shall, the verb never takes -s.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes will going or will playing.

example.question: Next week the school will ___ a match.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes the future with the -ing form heard in "I am going to".
misconceptions.reveals: will + an -ing verb among the options.
misconceptions.help: Will + plain verb. Or am going to + plain verb. Do not mix them.
misconceptions.feedback: After will and shall, use the plain verb, not the -ing form.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the present tense for a future event with a time word (Tomorrow I go).
misconceptions.cause: In speech the time word seems enough to show the future.
misconceptions.reveals: A future time word with a present tense verb among the options.
misconceptions.help: Tomorrow, next week and soon point to the future, so the verb needs will or shall.
misconceptions.feedback: A time word like tomorrow is not enough. Add will or shall before the verb to show the future.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses two helper verbs together (will shall go, will can).
misconceptions.cause: Combines two ways of speaking about the future.
misconceptions.reveals: will shall or will can among the options.
misconceptions.help: Choose one helper verb: will OR shall.
misconceptions.feedback: Use one helper verb only: will or shall, not both together.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of Writing: Punctuation (Theme 7: Learning through technology)
learning_experiences: read a short text and identify punctuation marks used collaboratively with peers,
use commas to show pauses between words, phrases or clauses,

Why do we punctuate sentences?
