sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills Education: effective communication is enhanced as the learner works collaboratively when picking out magazines, reading and identifying punctuation marks used.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the concept of correct punctuation in writing in all learning areas particularly in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify commas and double quotation marks in written texts
use the comma and double quotation marks correctly in sentences
advocate the use of correct punctuation in written communication

skills.name: Use the comma
skills.mastery: Puts commas between the items in a list, after an opening word or phrase and before the words a speaker says, and does not put a comma between a subject and its verb, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Punctuate direct speech with double quotation marks
skills.mastery: Puts double quotation marks round the exact words spoken, a capital letter at the start of the speech, and the comma, question mark or full stop inside the closing marks, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out commas in a list.

example.question: Mama bought maize flour sugar and tea.

misconceptions.cause: Does not see where one item ends.
misconceptions.reveals: A list written with no commas.
misconceptions.help: Put a comma after each item, except before and.
misconceptions.feedback: Put commas between the things in a list (before "and" you may leave it out).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a comma between the subject and the verb, or at every pause.

example.question: The children, played in the yard.

misconceptions.cause: Writes a comma wherever the voice stops.
misconceptions.reveals: A comma that splits a subject from its verb.
misconceptions.help: A comma is not a breath mark. Do not split who from what they did.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not put a comma between who and what they did. Commas are for lists and for separating parts.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the comma after an opening word or phrase (Yes I will; In the morning we left).
misconceptions.cause: Does not mark the end of an opening word.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence that starts with yes, no, well, or a time phrase and has no comma.
misconceptions.help: After Yes, No, Well or an opening phrase, add a comma.
misconceptions.feedback: Put a comma after an opening word such as Yes or No, and after a phrase that starts a sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Joins two full sentences with only a comma.

example.question: The bell rang, we ran outside.
example.correct_answer: The bell rang, and we ran

misconceptions.cause: Uses the comma as a full stop.
misconceptions.reveals: Two complete sentences with only a comma between them.
misconceptions.help: Use a full stop, or add and, but, so.
misconceptions.feedback: A comma cannot join two whole sentences alone. Use a full stop, or add a joining word.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: whether comma splice is taught at Grade 5

misconceptions.error: Writes spoken words with no quotation marks.
misconceptions.cause: Does not mark where speech begins and ends.
misconceptions.reveals: The spoken words with no marks.
misconceptions.help: Put double quotation marks around the exact words spoken.
misconceptions.feedback: Put double quotation marks round the exact words someone says.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the quotation marks round the words said and the speaker too.
misconceptions.cause: Does not see where the speech stops.
misconceptions.reveals: Quotation marks that include said + name.
misconceptions.help: Only the spoken words go between the marks.
misconceptions.feedback: Only the words the person said go inside the quotation marks, not "said Mother".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the comma, question mark or full stop outside the closing marks.
misconceptions.cause: Sees the end punctuation as part of the sentence, not of the speech.
misconceptions.reveals: A comma outside the closing marks, or a missing question mark.
misconceptions.help: The mark that ends the spoken words goes inside the quotation marks.
misconceptions.feedback: The comma, question mark or exclamation mark that ends the speech goes inside the closing quotation marks.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Starts the spoken words with a small letter.
misconceptions.cause: Treats the speech as the middle of the sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: Spoken words that begin with a small letter.
misconceptions.help: The first word of the spoken words starts with a capital letter.
misconceptions.feedback: The first word the speaker says begins with a capital letter.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses single quotation marks.
misconceptions.cause: Single quotation marks are used in some books and the learner copies them.
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence with single marks.
misconceptions.help: The Grade 5 design asks for double quotation marks: " ".
misconceptions.feedback: Your teacher wants double quotation marks " " for speech.
misconceptions.source: KICD Grade 5 design: double quotation marks (single marks are valid British style; to confirm with the teacher)

misconceptions.error: Ends the spoken words with a full stop when the speaker is named after them.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the spoken words are a complete sentence on their own.
misconceptions.reveals: A full stop before said + name.
misconceptions.help: When said + name follows, end the speech with a comma (or ? or !).
misconceptions.feedback: When "said" and the speaker follow the spoken words, end the speech with a comma, not a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 8: The farm-cash crops)

Which proverbs and sayings do you know?

skills.name: Know proverbs and their meanings
skills.mastery: Matches a common English proverb to its meaning, finishes a proverb, and uses it for the situation it fits, in 8 of 10 new questions.

misconceptions.error: Takes the proverb literally.

example.question: What does "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush" mean?
example.correct_answer: Be happy with what you have.

misconceptions.cause: Reads the words and not the lesson.
misconceptions.reveals: A literal reading among the options.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what lesson does the saying teach about people?
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb has a hidden lesson. Ask what it teaches people, not what the words say.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a lesson that is related but not the proverb's.
misconceptions.cause: Remembers the general topic but not the exact lesson.
misconceptions.reveals: A situation about teamwork that fits another saying better.
misconceptions.help: Match the lesson, not the topic.
misconceptions.feedback: This is on a similar topic, but the lesson is different. Match the exact lesson.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes the words of two proverbs.

example.question: Finish the proverb: A stitch in time saves ___.

misconceptions.cause: Remembers the shape and not the exact words.
misconceptions.reveals: A number or word from another proverb.
misconceptions.help: Say the proverb aloud three times and listen for the ending.
misconceptions.feedback: The proverb has fixed words. Say the whole proverb aloud to remember its ending.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Fluency in Reading (Theme 8: The farm-cash crops)
learning_experiences: scan through paragraphs for unfarmiliar words collaboratively,
search for an article on a topic they enjoy, select a portion to read,

participate in a reader’s theatre using a short text from a poem or short play, o select a story or poem that can be divided into parts or characters, o assign a portion to each member with peers, o read a portion of the script orally for practice, o read the assigned parts with peers,

sub_strands.sub_strand: Sentences (Theme 8: The farm-cash crops)
content_topics: Question Tags on the ‘Verb to be’
learning_experiences: fill in gaps in sentences using double imperatives,
select question tags from a story, dialogue or poem,
match statements with the correct question tag,
practise giving instructions related to the theme using double imperatives such as: shut down your tablets and listen to the teacher. Type this word in your tablet and look up its meaning,
role play giving and receiving of instructions at home using double imperatives,
use double imperatives to make rules for their classroom and display them in charts or posters,
write correct sentences using double imperatives.
key_inquiry_questions: What are some of your school rules?
How do you give instructions?
Why do we ask questions?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy is fostered as the learner formulates school or class rules using double imperatives.
sub_strands.values: Respect is developed as the learner practises using question tags and giving instructions in different contexts.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skill Education: Effective communication is developed as the learner role plays giving and receiving of instructions at home using double imperatives.
sub_strands.links: The learner applies the knowledge of imperatives to the same concept in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify questions tags and double imperatives from a text
use question tags and double imperatives correctly in sentences
advocate the correct use of double imperatives and question tags in communication

skills.name: Use question tags
skills.mastery: Adds the right question tag to a statement: the same helper verb, the opposite sign (is/isn't, does/doesn't, can/can't), and a pronoun, never the same tag for every sentence, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Uses "isn't it?" after every statement.

example.question: You are coming to the party, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Treats the tag as one fixed phrase.
misconceptions.reveals: isn't it offered after a statement with you, they, we or a different helper verb.
misconceptions.help: Repeat the helper verb from the statement, then the pronoun: are you coming, ... aren't you.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag copies the helper verb and the person of the statement. It is not always "isn't it".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; widespread in East African and South Asian English

misconceptions.error: Uses a tag with the same sign as the statement (He is tall, is he?).
misconceptions.cause: Does not know that the tag reverses positive and negative.
misconceptions.reveals: A tag with the same sign as the statement.
misconceptions.help: A positive statement takes a negative tag. A negative statement takes a positive tag.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag has the opposite sign. A positive statement takes a negative tag (doesn't he), a negative one takes a positive tag.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a different helper verb in the tag (She likes tea, isn't she?).
misconceptions.cause: Does not link the tag to the verb in the statement.
misconceptions.reveals: A tag with a helper verb that is not in the statement.
misconceptions.help: If the statement has likes, the tag uses does. If it has is, the tag uses is.
misconceptions.feedback: The helper verb in the tag must match the statement: likes goes with does/doesn't, can goes with can/can't.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Repeats the noun in the tag instead of a pronoun.
misconceptions.cause: Copies the subject word for word.
misconceptions.reveals: A noun inside the tag.
misconceptions.help: The tag uses a short word for the person: he, she, it, they.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag uses a pronoun (he, she, it, they), not the name.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the tag in full (is not he) or in the wrong order (he isn't).
misconceptions.cause: Does not know the tag turns the helper verb in front of the pronoun and is said short.
misconceptions.reveals: A tag written in full or in statement order.
misconceptions.help: Say it the way people speak: isn't it, doesn't she. The helper verb comes first.
misconceptions.feedback: A tag puts the short form first (isn't it), then the pronoun, as one quick question.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing (Theme 8: The farm-cash crops)

skills.name: Identify and use similes
skills.mastery: Spots a simile (a comparison with like or as), completes a common simile (as brave as a lion) and tells a simile from a plain statement or a metaphor, in 8 of 10 new questions.

misconceptions.error: Takes any description for a simile.

example.question: Which sentence is a simile?
example.correct_answer: He is as strong as an ox.

misconceptions.cause: Does not look for like or as.
misconceptions.reveals: A plain description beside a comparison.
misconceptions.help: A simile compares two different things using like or as.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile compares two things using "like" or "as". This sentence does not.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes a metaphor (without like or as) for a simile.

example.question: Which sentence is a simile?
example.correct_answer: He is as brave as a lion.

misconceptions.cause: Sees a comparison and does not check the joining word.
misconceptions.reveals: A metaphor beside a simile.
misconceptions.help: A simile has like or as. A metaphor says one thing IS another.
misconceptions.feedback: This is a metaphor. A simile always has the word "like" or "as".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Completes a simile with a word that does not fit the quality.
misconceptions.cause: Does not match the animal to the quality.
misconceptions.reveals: An animal known for a different quality.
misconceptions.help: Which animal or thing is famous for this quality?
misconceptions.feedback: This animal or thing is not known for this quality. Think about who is famous for it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

outcomes.text: identify the main idea in each paragraph
visualise events, characters and descriptions in texts for comprehension
summarise the main points in a text
answer direct and inferential questions for comprehension
challenge others to focus on detail when reading a text

skills.name: Find the main idea of a paragraph
skills.mastery: Chooses the sentence or title that covers the whole paragraph, and does not pick one detail or an idea the paragraph does not discuss, in 8 of 10 new passages.
question_forms: short comprehension: choose the main idea

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Summarise the main points
skills.mastery: Chooses the summary that keeps the main points in order and leaves out the small details and the writer's own opinion, in 8 of 10 new passages.
question_forms: choose what a summary leaves out

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks one detail as the main idea.

example.question: What is the main idea of the paragraph?

misconceptions.cause: Chooses the sentence that was easiest to find.
misconceptions.reveals: A true detail from the paragraph.
misconceptions.help: The main idea covers the whole paragraph. A detail covers only one part.
misconceptions.feedback: This is a true detail, but it is only one part. The main idea covers the whole paragraph.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a statement that is too wide for the paragraph.

example.question: What is the main idea of the paragraph?

misconceptions.cause: Chooses a big idea the paragraph only touches.
misconceptions.reveals: A statement about the whole subject, bigger than the paragraph.
misconceptions.help: The main idea fits this paragraph, not the whole topic.
misconceptions.feedback: This is too wide. The paragraph talks about one part of it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an idea that the paragraph does not discuss.

example.question: Which title best fits the paragraph?

misconceptions.cause: Chooses from background knowledge.
misconceptions.reveals: An idea on the same subject but not in the paragraph.
misconceptions.help: Check that the title matches what the paragraph says.
misconceptions.feedback: This idea is not in the paragraph. Check what the paragraph is actually about.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a summary that retells every detail.
misconceptions.cause: Believes a longer answer is better.
misconceptions.reveals: A summary almost as long as the passage.
misconceptions.help: A summary is shorter and keeps only the main points.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary should be short. This one keeps too many small details.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a summary that leaves out a main point.

example.question: Which is the best summary?
example.wrong_answer: a summary missing a main point

misconceptions.cause: Takes the first half of the passage only.
misconceptions.reveals: A summary that stops half way.
misconceptions.help: Check that every main point is in your summary.
misconceptions.feedback: This summary leaves out an important part. A good summary covers all the main points.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds an opinion or an idea that is not in the passage.

example.question: Which is the best summary?
example.correct_answer: a summary of the passage only

misconceptions.cause: Adds what he or she thinks.
misconceptions.reveals: A summary with a judging word such as best, silly, lazy.
misconceptions.help: A summary tells what the passage says, not what you think.
misconceptions.feedback: A summary only says what the passage says. This one adds an opinion.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a main point and keeps a small detail.

example.question: Which sentence is a small detail that a summary can leave out?

misconceptions.cause: Cannot tell main points from details.
misconceptions.reveals: A main point offered as the one to leave out.
misconceptions.help: Main points say what happens or what the text is about. Details add colour.
misconceptions.feedback: This is a main point, and a summary needs it. Choose the small detail that adds only colour.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

Creativity and Imagination is achieved as the learner engages in creative activities like creating crossword puzzles using different types of adverbs.

sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the knowledge gained in different types of adverbs to learn similar concept in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify adverbs of manner, time, place and frequency in a text
use adverbs correctly in oral and written contexts

skills.name: Identify and use adverbs of manner, time, place and frequency
skills.mastery: Tells whether an adverb shows manner, time, place or frequency, and uses the adverb (not the adjective) after the verb (runs quickly, sings well), in 8 of 10 new sentences.
question_forms: say what the adverb tells us

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use could and would
skills.mastery: Uses could for past ability or a polite request and would for a polite request or an imagined result, followed by the base verb, and builds how many ... could/would questions, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective after the verb (runs quick, speaks soft).
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili uses one word for both (haraka).
misconceptions.reveals: The adjective form among the options after a verb.
misconceptions.help: Ask: how did he run? The word describes the verb, so add -ly.
misconceptions.feedback: A word that tells HOW something is done describes the verb, so it needs the adverb form (quickly).
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses good where well is needed (sings good).
misconceptions.cause: Treats good as the adverb of well.
misconceptions.reveals: good among the options after a verb.
misconceptions.help: Good describes a noun (a good singer). Well describes a verb (sings well).
misconceptions.feedback: Good describes a noun. After a verb, use well.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses hardly for hard (works hardly).

example.question: The farmers work ___ in the shamba.

misconceptions.cause: Adds -ly to every adjective to make an adverb.
misconceptions.reveals: hardly among the options.
misconceptions.help: Hard stays hard: works hard. Hardly means almost not at all.
misconceptions.feedback: The adverb of hard is hard. Hardly means "almost not at all".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the kinds of adverb (time, frequency, place, manner).

example.question: In "She often visits her aunt", often tells us ___.

misconceptions.cause: Sees "when" in every adverb that is about time.
misconceptions.reveals: A frequency word offered with time as an option.
misconceptions.help: Frequency answers how often: always, never, often, sometimes. Time answers when: today, soon.
misconceptions.feedback: Always, often, sometimes and never tell HOW OFTEN (frequency). Time words tell WHEN.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the adverb of frequency in the wrong place (She is late always).
misconceptions.cause: Places the adverb at the end as in Kiswahili (huchelewa kila mara).
misconceptions.reveals: A frequency word at the end of the sentence among the options.
misconceptions.help: Frequency words usually go before the main verb, but after is, am, are.
misconceptions.feedback: A frequency adverb usually goes before the main verb, but after is, am, are and was.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses can to talk about the past.

example.question: When I was five, I ___ climb trees.

misconceptions.cause: Does not change can for the past.
misconceptions.reveals: can in a sentence that begins with a past time.
misconceptions.help: Can is now. Could is the past of can.
misconceptions.feedback: Talk about the past with could: when I was five, I could climb trees.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses will for an imagined result (If I had money, I will buy).

example.question: If I had a bicycle, I ___ ride to school.

misconceptions.cause: Does not match the if-part in the past with would in the result.
misconceptions.reveals: will after an if-part in the past tense.
misconceptions.help: If + past tense, then would + verb.
misconceptions.feedback: When the if-part is in the past tense, the result uses would, not will.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a past tense after could or would (could went).
misconceptions.cause: Thinks the past needs two past words.
misconceptions.reveals: could/would + a past form.
misconceptions.help: Could already shows the past. The verb after it stays plain: could help.
misconceptions.feedback: After could and would, use the plain verb: could help, would go.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gets the order wrong in how many ... could/would questions.
misconceptions.cause: Does not keep how many together.
misconceptions.reveals: How and many split apart.
misconceptions.help: Keep how many together, then could, then the person, then the verb.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep "how many" together, then could/would, then the person: How many eggs could you carry?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of Writing: Punctuation Marks (Theme 9: Communicable diseases)
learning_experiences: listen to a short oral text and write the text with the correct punctuation marks
underline the apostrophe and exclamation marks in a text with peers,
construct sentences using the apostrophe and exclamation mark,
watch online videos or slides about the correct use of the apostrophe and exclamation mark,
create and display charts or posters with sentences in which the apostrophe and exclamation mark are used collaboratively with peers,
conduct a gallery walk and view the charts made by each group of peers.
key_inquiry_questions: Which punctuation marks do you know?
Why do we punctuate sentences?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination is enriched as the learner develops and displays posters and charts in the classroom for peers to review.
Learning to Learn is developed as the learner searches for information on the internet and learns surfing skills.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is developed as the learner creates and displays charts using different types of sentences and punctuates them correctly.
sub_strands.pcis: Health Education is enhanced as the learner interacts with material on common communicable diseases both offline and online.
sub_strands.links: Punctuation marks are used in all areas of learning as the learner takes down notes. Kiswahili in particular is an area that the learner can apply this concept, as it teaches on punctuation as a skill.

outcomes.text: identify the apostrophe and exclamation mark in sentences
punctuate sentences correctly using the apostrophe and the exclamation mark
collaborate with others to punctuate own or provided documents

skills.name: Use the apostrophe
skills.mastery: Uses the apostrophe for belonging (Juma's bag, the girls' room) and for missing letters (don't, it's), tells its from it's, and does not put an apostrophe in a plain plural (banana's), in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use the exclamation mark
skills.mastery: Ends a sentence of strong feeling, surprise, warning or a shout with an exclamation mark, keeps the full stop for ordinary statements and the question mark for questions, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Puts an apostrophe in a plain plural (banana's for sale).
misconceptions.cause: Thinks every s needs an apostrophe.
misconceptions.reveals: An apostrophe in a plural with no owner.
misconceptions.help: An apostrophe shows belonging or missing letters, never just more than one.
misconceptions.feedback: An apostrophe is not for a plain plural. Write bananas, books, boys.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up its (belonging) and it's (it is).
misconceptions.cause: Both sound the same and both look as if they need an apostrophe.
misconceptions.reveals: its and it's offered together.
misconceptions.help: Say it is. If it fits, it's. If not, its.
misconceptions.feedback: Try "it is" in the gap. If it does not fit, you need its (belonging), with no apostrophe.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the apostrophe when something belongs to someone (Jumas bag).
misconceptions.cause: Does not mark belonging in writing.
misconceptions.reveals: A noun with s and no apostrophe where belonging is meant.
misconceptions.help: Add apostrophe and s to show belonging: Juma's bag.
misconceptions.feedback: To show that something belongs to Juma, add an apostrophe and s: Juma's.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the apostrophe in don't or puts it in the wrong place (do'nt).
misconceptions.cause: Does not mark the missing letter.
misconceptions.reveals: dont or do'nt among the options.
misconceptions.help: The apostrophe sits where the letter is missing: do not becomes don't.
misconceptions.feedback: The apostrophe goes where a letter is missing: do not becomes don't.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the apostrophe before the s when the owners are plural (the girl's room, for many girls), or the reverse.

example.question: The ___ room is next to ours. (many girls)

misconceptions.cause: Does not ask if one or many own it.
misconceptions.reveals: girl's and girls' offered together.
misconceptions.help: One owner: 's. Many owners ending in s: s'.
misconceptions.feedback: One owner: apostrophe then s. Many owners whose name ends in s: s then apostrophe.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: whether plural possessives are taught at Grade 5

misconceptions.error: Uses a full stop after a shout, a warning or a strong feeling.
misconceptions.cause: Treats every sentence the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A warning or a cry that ends in a full stop.
misconceptions.help: A shout, a warning and strong surprise need !
misconceptions.feedback: A warning, shout or strong feeling needs an exclamation mark.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an exclamation mark after calm, ordinary sentences.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks ! makes writing more exciting.
misconceptions.reveals: A calm statement ending in !
misconceptions.help: Keep ! for strong feeling. A calm statement ends in a full stop.
misconceptions.feedback: A calm sentence ends with a full stop. Save the exclamation mark for strong feeling.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes more than one exclamation mark (!!!).
misconceptions.cause: Copies the style of messages on phones.
misconceptions.reveals: More than one ! at the end of a sentence.
misconceptions.help: One mark is enough in school writing.
misconceptions.feedback: One exclamation mark is enough.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends a real question with an exclamation mark.
misconceptions.cause: Writes a strong voice as ! even for a question.
misconceptions.reveals: A question that ends in !
misconceptions.help: A question that asks something ends with ?
misconceptions.feedback: A question that asks for an answer ends with a question mark.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary: Interactive Listening (Theme 10: Leisure time activities)
learning_experiences: listen to a narrative and retell it while expressing different moods or feelings,
construct sentences collaboratively with peers,
say words containing the sounds /s/ and /z/ with peers,
watch a video of a conversational narrative or a choral verse online or offline,
take turns pick out words that show polite interruption in the video,
engage in a dialogue and practise interrupting one another politely.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should you interrupt others politely?
How do you show different moods and feelings when listening to someone?
Which words do you use to join an on-going conversation?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration is fostered as the learner works with peers to construct sentences orally.
Creativity and Imagination is enhanced as the learner creates and role plays conversations and takes turn during a conversation.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility is promoted as the learner engages in a dialogue and practises interrupting one another politely.

sub_strands.links: The learner applies the skill of conversing in dialogue form to Kiswahili as it has similar concepts.

outcomes.text: identify different moods in a narrative or a choral verse
use words and phrases with the selected sound /s/ and /z/ in sentences

skills.name: Tell the mood or feeling in a narrative
skills.mastery: Reads a few lines of a narrative and names the feeling or mood, using the words and actions as evidence, and does not name the opposite feeling from one cheerful or sad word, in 8 of 10 new extracts.

misconceptions.error: Names the opposite feeling from one cheerful or sad word.

example.question: Wafula laughed, but his hands shook. He felt ___.

misconceptions.cause: Reads one word (laughed) and ignores the rest.
misconceptions.reveals: A mood that matches one word and not the others.
misconceptions.help: Check what the person does and says, not just one word.
misconceptions.feedback: One word does not tell the whole feeling. Check what the person does and says.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names a feeling that is not supported by the lines.
misconceptions.cause: Picks a strong feeling without evidence.
misconceptions.reveals: A strong feeling with no supporting words.
misconceptions.help: Find the words and actions that show the feeling.
misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the lines shows this feeling. Look for words and actions that show how the person feels.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: skim through a text and obtain the main idea,

Why should we make notes when reading?

sub_strands.links: The learner applies the skill of intensive reading to Kiswahili where such a skill is emphasised.

outcomes.text: relate the ideas in a text to their experiences for comprehension
respond to direct and inferential questions from a text correctly

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Class: Conjunctions (Theme 10: Leisure time activities)
learning_experiences: listen to a short dialogue and identify conjunctions,
make sentences from a substitution table using but, or, yet, because, since and also,
construct sentences using conjunctions with peers,
fill in blank spaces using conjunctions in sentences or paragraphs,
create a display chart of sentences containing conjunctions with peers,
conduct a gallery walk and give feedback to each group.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do you join words and sentences?
How do you join words or sentences?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Collaboration is enhanced as the learner constructs sentences using conjunctions collaboratively with peers.
Creativity and imagination is developed as the learner creates a display chart and conducts a gallery walk giving feedback on the displayed charts.

outcomes.text: identify conjunctions: but, or, yet, because, since and also, in texts for effective communication
use conjunctions but, or, yet, because, since and also, correctly in communication
judge the correctness and appropriateness of conjunctions in oral and written texts

skills.name: Join sentences with but, or, yet, because, since and also
skills.mastery: Chooses the conjunction that fits the meaning (contrast, choice, reason) and uses only one joining word in a sentence (not Because ..., so ...), in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Uses because where but (a contrast) is needed.

example.question: Ali is small, ___ he runs very fast.

misconceptions.cause: Joins two ideas without asking how they relate.
misconceptions.reveals: because/so offered where the second idea is a surprise.
misconceptions.help: Ask: is the second part a reason, a surprise or a choice?
misconceptions.feedback: Read both parts. If the second part is a surprise after the first, use but or yet, not because.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses two joining words together (Because ..., so ...; Although ..., but ...).

example.question: Because it was raining, so we stayed home.

misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili uses two joining words (kwa sababu... kwa hivyo).
misconceptions.reveals: A sentence with both because and so.
misconceptions.help: One joining word per sentence. Because it rained, we stayed. Or: It rained, so we stayed.
misconceptions.feedback: Use ONE joining word between two ideas. Because and so do the same job, so use only one.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses and where or (a choice) is needed.
misconceptions.cause: Treats and as the only joining word.
misconceptions.reveals: and offered when two things are being chosen between.
misconceptions.help: A choice between two things uses or.
misconceptions.feedback: When you choose one of two things, use "or", not "and".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses since only for time and misses its meaning of because.

example.question: We stayed indoors ___ it was raining.

misconceptions.cause: Learns only the time meaning of since.
misconceptions.reveals: Since as a reason offered or rejected.
misconceptions.help: Since can mean because. Since I was five means a time. Since it rained means a reason.
misconceptions.feedback: Since can mean "because" (a reason) or "from a time". Read the meaning.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: whether since for a reason is taught at Grade 5

misconceptions.error: Uses also as if it joined two words (tea also coffee).
misconceptions.cause: Thinks also is another way to say and.
misconceptions.reveals: also between two nouns.
misconceptions.help: Also adds an idea in a new sentence or after the verb. And joins two words.
misconceptions.feedback: "Also" does not join two nouns. Use "and", or begin a new sentence with Also.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a joining word that does not fit the meaning of the two parts.
misconceptions.cause: Treats all joining words as the same.
misconceptions.reveals: A joining word whose meaning does not fit the two ideas.
misconceptions.help: Say the two parts and ask: do they add, contrast, give a reason or offer a choice?
misconceptions.feedback: Read both parts of the sentence. This joining word does not fit what the two parts mean together.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Use of Interrogatives (Theme 11: Sports - appreciating talents)

use the wh- words and how to ask questions collaboratively,
construct questions using the pattern: how much more..., when/who/why/what else with peers for example, who else attended the ceremony? how much more sugar was bought?

outcomes.text: identify interrogatives: how, what, when, why, who in sentences correctly
use interrogatives how much more..., when/who/why/what else accurately in sentences
adopt the use of interrogatives used in oral and written texts

skills.name: Ask questions with how, what, when, why, who
skills.mastery: Chooses the question word that fits the answer given, puts the helper verb before the subject (What are you doing?), and uses how much more and when/who/why/what else correctly, in 8 of 10 new questions.

misconceptions.error: Uses who for things or what for people.
misconceptions.cause: Does not ask whether the answer is a person or a thing.
misconceptions.reveals: who and what swapped in a question about a person or a thing.
misconceptions.help: A person: who. A thing or idea: what.
misconceptions.feedback: Who asks about people. What asks about things.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes when (time), where (place) and why (reason).

example.question: "___ did you arrive late?" "Because the bus broke down."

misconceptions.cause: Does not read the answer to see what is being asked.
misconceptions.reveals: An answer that is a reason, a time or a place beside the wrong question word.
misconceptions.help: Because gives a reason: why. At six o'clock gives a time: when.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at the answer. An answer that begins with because is a reason, so the question word is why.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps statement order in a question (What you are doing?).
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili questions keep the same word order as statements.
misconceptions.reveals: A question with the subject before the helper verb.
misconceptions.help: In a question, the helper verb comes first: are you, did he, can she.
misconceptions.feedback: In a question the helper verb comes before the subject: What are you doing?
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Leaves out do, does or did (Why you came late?).
misconceptions.cause: Drops the helper verb as in quick speech.
misconceptions.reveals: A question with no do, does or did.
misconceptions.help: With most verbs the question needs did, do or does, and the verb goes back to plain.
misconceptions.feedback: Most questions need do, does or did. Then the verb goes plain: Why did you come late?
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Puts else in the wrong place or adds another word (what other else).
misconceptions.cause: Adds a second word of the same meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: else with other or more.
misconceptions.help: Else already means "in addition". Use one word: who else, what else.
misconceptions.feedback: Else means "in addition". Use it alone after who, what, when or why.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes how much (cannot be counted) and how many (can be counted).
misconceptions.cause: Does not ask whether the thing can be counted.
misconceptions.reveals: how much with a countable noun, or how many with an uncountable one.
misconceptions.help: Goats can be counted: how many. Rice cannot be counted one by one: how much.
misconceptions.feedback: Use how many for things you can count (goats) and how much for things you cannot count (rice, milk).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Spell and use homophones
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word from a pair or trio of words that sound alike (there/their, to/too/two, hear/here, write/right, piece/peace) from the meaning of the sentence, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Use homonyms in the right meaning
skills.mastery: Recognises that one spelling can carry two meanings (bank, bat, bark, light, match) and picks the sentence that uses the word in the meaning asked for, in 8 of 10 new questions.
question_forms: choose the sentence with this meaning
choose the meaning in a sentence

misconceptions.error: Mixes there, their and they're.

example.question: The children left ___ bags in the classroom.

misconceptions.cause: The three words sound the same.
misconceptions.reveals: there/their/they're in one sentence.
misconceptions.help: Their means belonging to them. There is a place. They're means they are.
misconceptions.feedback: Their shows that something belongs to them. There shows a place. They're means "they are".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes to, too and two.
misconceptions.cause: The three words sound the same.
misconceptions.reveals: to/too/two in one sentence.
misconceptions.help: Two is the number. Too means also or more than needed. To is a direction word.
misconceptions.feedback: Two is the number 2. Too means "also" or "more than enough". To shows where or what for.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses by sound alone, so picks whichever spelling comes to mind.
misconceptions.cause: Does not stop to think about the meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Two words that sound the same where the meaning decides.
misconceptions.help: Say what the word means, then match it to the spelling: piece is a part, peace is calm.
misconceptions.feedback: The words sound the same but mean different things. Think about the meaning to choose the spelling.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes up hear and here, write and right, see and sea.
misconceptions.cause: Knows both spellings but not which meaning each carries.
misconceptions.reveals: hear/here, write/right, see/sea, meet/meat.
misconceptions.help: Hear has an ear in it. Here is about a place, like there.
misconceptions.feedback: Hear is what you do with your ears. Here means "in this place".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the commonest meaning of the word and ignores the one asked for.

example.question: Which sentence uses bank to mean the side of a river?
example.wrong_answer: He saved money at the bank.
example.correct_answer: We sat on the bank of the river.

misconceptions.cause: Knows only the first meaning learned.
misconceptions.reveals: The common meaning among the options next to the less common.
misconceptions.help: Read the whole sentence before you choose.
misconceptions.feedback: This word has more than one meaning. Read the question and the rest of the sentence to see which meaning is used.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Matches on the word alone and does not check the other words in the sentence.

example.question: Which sentence uses bat to mean the animal that flies at night?
example.wrong_answer: The batsman hit the ball with his bat.
example.correct_answer: A bat flew out of the cave at dusk.

misconceptions.cause: Sees the same spelling and stops.
misconceptions.reveals: Two sentences with the same word and different surrounding clues.
misconceptions.help: Look for clue words: cave, night, wings; or ball, cricket.
misconceptions.feedback: Check the other words in the sentence. They show which meaning is used.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use nouns that are the same in singular and plural
skills.mastery: Uses sheep, fish, deer, aircraft, series and species (and does not write sheeps or deers), keeps the verb in agreement with the number meant, and still writes the irregular plurals children, men, feet and teeth, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to a noun that does not change (sheeps, deers, aircrafts).
misconceptions.cause: Applies the regular plural rule to every noun.
misconceptions.reveals: sheeps, deers and fishs among the options.
misconceptions.help: A few words stay the same: sheep, deer, fish, series, species, aircraft.
misconceptions.feedback: Sheep, deer, fish, series, species and aircraft stay the same in the plural.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to an irregular plural (childs, mans, foots, tooths).
misconceptions.cause: Applies the regular plural rule to a word that changes inside.
misconceptions.reveals: childs, mans, foots among the options.
misconceptions.help: Learn these by heart: child-children, man-men, foot-feet, tooth-teeth.
misconceptions.feedback: Some plurals change the whole word: child becomes children, man becomes men, foot becomes feet.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a singular verb with many sheep or fish (The sheep is grazing).
misconceptions.cause: Sees the noun without -s and takes it as singular.
misconceptions.reveals: A number before a same-form noun, and a singular verb.
misconceptions.help: Look for a number or many. Fifty sheep are; one sheep is.
misconceptions.feedback: The number tells you if it is one or many. With fifty sheep, the verb is plural: are.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a or one before a plural form (a sheeps; one fishes).
misconceptions.cause: Does not link a/an to a single thing.
misconceptions.reveals: a/an with a plural form.
misconceptions.help: A fish is one. Fish can also mean many, with a number: five fish.
misconceptions.feedback: The word "a" is for one thing only, so the noun is singular: a fish.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use in, on and at for time and place
skills.mastery: Chooses in, on or at for times (at 8 o'clock, on Monday, in June) and places (at the gate, on the table, in the room), in 8 of 10 new sentences.

skills.name: Use into, towards, to and through for direction
skills.mastery: Chooses into, towards, to or through for movement, and does not write to home or entered into, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

misconceptions.error: Uses in or at for a day or date (in Monday, at Saturday).
misconceptions.cause: Uses one preposition for all times.
misconceptions.reveals: in/at beside a day of the week or a date.
misconceptions.help: On for days and dates. At for clock times and moments. In for months, years and parts of the day.
misconceptions.feedback: Use "on" with days and dates: on Monday, on 12 June.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses in or on for a clock time (in 8 o'clock).
misconceptions.cause: Uses in for every time.
misconceptions.reveals: in or on beside a clock time.
misconceptions.help: At for exact clock times and for night: at 8 o'clock, at night.
misconceptions.feedback: Use "at" for exact times and for night: at 8 o'clock, at night.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses at or on for parts of the day, months and years (at the morning).

example.question: I wake up early ___ the morning.

misconceptions.cause: Translates the Kiswahili phrase for each time word with the same word.
misconceptions.reveals: at/on beside morning, afternoon, evening, a month or a year.
misconceptions.help: In for morning, afternoon, evening, months, years and seasons.
misconceptions.feedback: Use "in" with the morning, afternoon and evening, with months and with years.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Mixes in, on and at for places (on the room, at the table in).
misconceptions.cause: Does not think about how the thing sits in the place.
misconceptions.reveals: in/at beside a surface or a point.
misconceptions.help: On touches a surface, in is inside, at is a point or place.
misconceptions.feedback: Use "on" for a thing resting on a surface, "in" for inside, and "at" for a point or a place such as the gate.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes to home (went to home).
misconceptions.cause: Kiswahili says kwenda nyumbani; the word for to is built into the verb.
misconceptions.reveals: to home among the options.
misconceptions.help: Home needs no to: go home, come home, walk home.
misconceptions.feedback: The word "home" already tells where. Say "went home", not "went to home".
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes entered into for walking into a place.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes into (movement) with the verb enter, which has the meaning built in.
misconceptions.reveals: entered into among the options.
misconceptions.help: Enter already means go into. Say entered the room, or went into the room.
misconceptions.feedback: The verb "enter" already means "go into". Say "entered the classroom".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; widespread in East African English

misconceptions.error: Writes towards to, or uses to for a movement in the direction of.
misconceptions.cause: Joins two direction words.
misconceptions.reveals: towards to among the options.
misconceptions.help: Towards is already a direction word. Use it alone.
misconceptions.feedback: Towards is complete on its own. Do not add "to".
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes through (from one side to the other) with into (going inside).

example.question: The train went ___ a tunnel and came out the other side.

misconceptions.cause: Does not think about whether the movement ends inside or comes out.
misconceptions.reveals: into and through offered together.
misconceptions.help: Through goes in one side and out the other. Into stops inside.
misconceptions.feedback: Through goes in at one side and out at the other. Into only goes inside.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

outcomes.text: identify homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels correctly
spell homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels correctly

skills.name: Spell words with double consonants and double vowels
skills.mastery: Spells words such as summer, happy, address, letter, coffee, see, food, week and queen with the right doubled letters, in 8 of 10 new words, and chooses the correctly spelt word in a sentence.

prerequisites.reason: Proposed: this skill builds on it. To confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes one consonant where two are needed (sumer, leter).
misconceptions.cause: Spells by sound and does not hear the double letter.
misconceptions.reveals: A word spelt with one consonant among the options.
misconceptions.help: Learn the double letters in common words: summer, letter, happy, address.
misconceptions.feedback: This word has a double consonant. Look at the middle of the word again.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Doubles a letter that should be single, or doubles the wrong letter (adress, succes, comittee).

example.question: Please write your ___ on the form.

misconceptions.cause: Guesses which letter to double.
misconceptions.reveals: A word with the wrong letter doubled.
misconceptions.help: Check every double letter: address has dd and ss.
misconceptions.feedback: Check which letters are doubled. In this word, two different letters are doubled, or the doubled letter is not the one you chose.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes one vowel where two are needed (fod, shep, wek).
misconceptions.cause: Spells by the short sound.
misconceptions.reveals: A word with one vowel among the options.
misconceptions.help: The sound is long, so two vowels: oo, ee.
misconceptions.feedback: This word has a double vowel (oo or ee). The sound is long.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells a word the way it sounds (sucess, coffe).
misconceptions.cause: Spells by ear and does not remember the shape of the word.
misconceptions.reveals: A word that is a sound-for-sound spelling.
misconceptions.help: Say the word in syllables and write each: cof-fee.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not spell this word by sound alone. Look for the double letters.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

rubrics.heading: Suggested Assessment Rubric: Listening and Speaking

indicators.indicator: Ability to listen actively to a variety of oral texts to gain information.

levels.EE: Maintains meaningful eye-contact, sits upright, nods, takes notes, responds to oral questions correctly for information in a variety of contexts.
levels.ME: Maintains eye contact, sits upright, nods and takes notes for information in varied contexts.
levels.AE: Either maintains eye contact or sits upright or takes notes for information.
levels.BE: Yawns, looks out, has to be prompted while listening for information.

indicators.indicator: Ability to listen and participate actively in conversations in various settings for self-expression and effective communication.

levels.EE: Participates actively in conversations, observes proper turn-taking skills, nods, maintains meaningful eye contact in a variety of settings for effective communication.
levels.ME: Participates actively in conversations in various settings for self-expression and effective communication.
levels.BE: Shows outright disinterest in conversations. Yawns, doses and interrupts conversations.

indicators.indicator: Ability to speak accurately with expression and at the right speed, with minimum hesitation for fluency for effective communication.

levels.EE: Speaks accurately with expression and at the right speed without hesitation in varied contexts for effective communication.
levels.ME: Speaks accurately with expression and at the right speed, with minimum hesitation for fluency.
levels.AE: Speaks accurately with expression but at slow speed and with hesitation.
levels.BE: Speaks inaccurately without expression and at a slow speed with many hesitations.

indicators.indicator: Ability to read about 400 words fluently and accurately, at the right speed and with expression for effective communication. Ability to read the text and relate the ideas to real life experiences.

levels.EE: Reads more than 350 words in varied texts fluently, accurately and expressively for effective communication. Reads a variety of texts and relates the ideas to immediate contexts and real life experiences.
levels.ME: Reads about 300 words fluently and accurately at the right speed and with expression for effective communication. Reads the text and relates the ideas to real life experiences.
levels.AE: Reads about 800 words fluently and accurately at the right speed and with expression for effective communication. Reads the text and comprehends main idea but fails to relate to real life experiences.
levels.BE: Reads about 200 words fluently and accurately but at slow speed without expression. Reads the text but fails to grasp the main idea and relate to real life experiences.

indicators.indicator: Ability to select and read relevant materials of between 1000-1250 words for information and pleasure.

levels.EE: Selects and reads a variety of relevant materials of more than 1300 words for information and pleasure.
levels.ME: Selects and reads relevant materials of between 1000-1250 words for information and pleasure.
levels.AE: Selects and reads relevant materials of below 1000 words for information and pleasure.
levels.BE: Selects and reads relevant material of below 500 words and reads for information and pleasure.

rubrics.heading: Suggested Assessment Rubric: Grammar in Use

indicators.indicator: Ability to use grammatical forms to communicate ideas, opinions, and emotions appropriately in different settings for effective communication.

levels.EE: Uses grammatical forms to communicate ideas, opinions, and emotions appropriately at all times in different settings and contexts for effective communication.
levels.ME: Uses grammatical forms to communicate ideas, opinions, and emotions appropriately in different settings for effective communication.
levels.AE: Uses grammatical forms to communicate ideas, but not opinions and emotions.
levels.BE: Fails to use correct grammatical forms to communicate, ideas, opinions and emotions.

indicators.indicator: Ability to use punctuation, paragraphing and spelling correctly for effective communication.

levels.EE: Uses punctuation, paragraphing and spelling correctly for varied types of writing for effective communication.
levels.ME: Uses punctuation, paragraphing and spelling correctly for effective communication.
levels.AE: Uses either punctuation, paragraphing or spelling correctly.
levels.BE: Uses faulty paragraphing, poor punctuation and spelling when writing.

indicators.indicator: Ability to write a variety of writings using the correct formats for effective communication.

levels.EE: Writes a variety of writings using correct formats and uses appropriate language for varied writing tasks for effective communication.
levels.ME: Writes a variety of writings using the correct formats for effective communication.
levels.AE: Writes a number of writings using correct formats for effective communication.
levels.BE: Writes all the writings using wrong formats.

indicators.indicator: Ability to write creative works clearly and expressively for effective communication.

levels.EE: Writes a variety creative works clearly, expressively, pleasantly and convincingly for effective communication.
levels.ME: Writes creative works clearly and expressively for effective communication.
levels.AE: Writes a few of the creative works clearly but lacks expressive ability.
levels.BE: Writes all the creative works without clarity and expressiveness due to limited language ability.
